newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Chess supercomputer tuned for re-match.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chess supercomputer tuned for re-match.

text.p: The massive calculating power of IBM's chess-playing supercomputer Deep Blue has been imbued with a human touch for its next encounter with world champion Garry Kasparov, one of the most eagerly awaited re-matches in history.

The computer won one game and drew two others against Kasparov in their 1996 match in Philadelphia. The Russian grandmaster, considered by most experts to be the strongest player in the history of the ancient game, eventually won the 6-game contest, but the outcome left him shaken by the feeling that the days of human superiority over machines were numbered.

A victory for Deep Blue in the $1.1 million re-match May 3-11 could be the major breakthrough IBM's computer scientists have been labouring for years to achieve. "I think the major difference is that in the last match we brought a lot of technology and this time we're going to bring a lot of human input," computer scientist Hsu Feng-Hsiung told Reuters at IBM's T.J. Watson Research Centre in Yorktown Heights, New York.

The "human input" is the addition of grandmaster Joel Benjamin as a full-time adviser. Benjamin, who worked briefly on the 1996 match, has infused the system with more chess knowledge while working with scientists Hsu, Murray Campbell, Joseph Hoane, Jerry Brody and Tan Chung-Jen.

Throw more memory and twice the calculating speed into the mix, and the IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess is reprogrammed and ready for Kasparov, who has been king of chess for 12 years.

Kasparov, who turns 34 in April, has shown some of the best form of his career in recent months against his most formidable human challengers. He was undefeated in winning a tournament of the world's top six grandmasters in December and followed that up with several more virtuoso games in February to win the prestigious annual Linares tournament in Spain.
SCIENTISTS APPEAR CONFIDENT

"Going into the last match I think we had a lot of desire and at that time I would say, 'I think we could win,' but this time I believe we can win," said Hsu, 38, designer of the silicon microchips that accelerate Deep Blue's calculating speed.
The scientists' sole victory in Philadelphia was the first time a machine had defeated a world champion under traditional playing conditions in which games can last as long as 6 hours.

Tucked away in the woods of Westchester County north of New York City, the glass-enclosed IBM research centre is home to Deep Blue -- two 6-foot 5-inch (1.9 metre) tall modules each containing 16 processors. During games, they communicate with each other through switches and transmit the results of their calculations through telephone lines to a video display unit.

What was a fascinating experiment last year to further assess possible commercial uses of IBM's RS/6000 SP parallel processing systems has this year become more about winning at chess and showing off the company's technology.
"I understand that sometimes if it wins a pretty game that's great, but you know if it wins ugly it's still winning," Benjamin said. "If you can beat Kasparov any kind of way, it's beautiful."
DEEP BLUE FINE-TUNED FOR STRATEGY

IBM says Benjamin has helped the team augment the computer's ability to look at hundreds of millions of positions per second with a greater appreciation for strategy and the relative value of pieces in certain positions.

It was Kasparov's careful planning, combined with his vast experience and human intuition, that proved the computer's downfall in losing three games in the last match. Among the weaknesses the team believes it has corrected in the last 13 months was Deep Blue's tendency to allow Kasparov slowly to restrict the movement of its pieces.

Campbell and Hoane, sitting at a chess board in Benjamin's office, re-enacted the doomed position of last year's final game and explained how fine-tuning the system would prevent that from happening again. Deep Blue, a play on IBM's nickname Big Blue, had allowed Kasparov to squeeze its pieces into an awkward defensive posture that left it with a rook and bishop standing idle on the back rank.

"It knew the bishop had no squares to move to and yet it wasn't really worried about it. Nowadays, it would be very worried about that," said Campbell, 39, the only chess player among the five scientists.
The tuning process involved studying and changing how the programme appreciates pawns, rooks, knights, bishops, queen and king -- the pieces on a chess board.
"What you have to do is have an automatic process to do something like that," Hoane said. "This is a scientific research topic to tune a multi-varied system like this."

The 6-game re-match will be played at the Equitable Centre in Manhattan with $700,000 going to the winner and $400,000 to the loser. IBM is the sole sponsor with assistance from the Association of Computing and Machinery (ACM).
Team manager Tan, "CJ" as he is known, said one of the goals of the chess project was to see how chess can be used to understand computer science applications.

IBM chose three areas -- data mining, financial modelling techniques and molecular dynamics -- in which to market the technology developed for Deep Blue, an acceleration of the parallel processing systems already applied in many industries, corporations, government agencies and academic institutions.
The first match, part of ACM's 50th anniversary celebrations, drew hundreds of spectators and an estimated 5 million "hits" on an Internet Web site retrieved by people all over the world.
